sentences.text: Sillosuchus was a large reptile belonging to the shuvosaurid family, a group of bipedal, lightly armored animals with dinosaur-like hip and skull structures.
Despite being closely related to modern crocodilians, this archosaur likely possessed a toothless, beaked mouth and a notably long, slender neck.
Its skeleton featured large excavations on the neck and back vertebrae, short fused ischia flattened top-to-bottom, and deep cavities in the cervical bones possibly linked to pneumatic structures.
Sillosuchus longicervix holds the distinction of being the only named bipedal poposauroid known from outside North America.
The specific name longicervix highlights the genus's defining elongated cervical vertebrae, which contained deep cavities called pleuroceli.
One specimen preserves a large isolated cervical vertebra measuring exactly 20 cm in length.
The genus was formally described in 1997 by paleontologists Oscar Alcober and J. Michael Parrish based on the holotype found in the Ischigualasto Formation.
These remains were unearthed in the province of San Juan, Argentina, a region inhabited by the animal during the Late Triassic period.

Additional fragments were initially attributed to Saurosuchus by Dr. William Sill in 1974, but a 2011 re-evaluation by Nesbitt confirmed they shared distinctive features with the holotype while being much larger.
Comparative studies suggest Sillosuchus maintained a light body and a bipedal posture, a conclusion drawn despite the lack of complete skull remains.
Based on related species, this herbivore lived in a warm, seasonal environment featuring river-crossed alluvial plains and abundant vegetation.
A 2026 study by Ponce, Cerda, and Desojo analyzed the histology of limb bones in Sillosuchus longicervix to investigate diverse growth rates among pseudosuchians.
Sillosuchus belongs to the family Shuvosauridae within the broader group Poposauroidea.
It is classified as a member of Poposauridae, an archosaur clade in Pseudosuchia more closely related to crocodilians than to dinosaurs, a position confirmed by a 2011 analysis by Sterling Nesbitt.
This animal lived during the Carnian stage, between 237 and 227.3 million years ago, in South America.
It is debated whether the long neck of Sillosuchus was a unique trait or simply typical for shuvosaurids.
